name: Kabyle
confidence_why: The class-dependent placement (noun group on the penult, verb group on the last full vowel, as a pitch peak) rests on Chaker's 1991 one-speaker instrumental study, which itself concludes that Kabyle has no intrinsic word accent; Willms 1965 (as summarized in Vycichl and Chaker 1984) also makes the position depend on word class but puts the noun accent on the initial syllable as an intensity accen…

catalog_quote: Le kabyle possède un accent de mot de nature mélodique. C’est, pratiquement dans tous les cas (72 sur 77, soit ± 93,5 %), la fréquence fondamentale (F°) qui est le facteur discriminant [...] L’immense majorité des nominaux (isolés) sont des paroxytons : l’accent porte très régulièrement sur l’avant-dernière syllabe. [...] Dans les trisyllabiques, l’accent sera normalement situé sur la syllabe médiane. [...] la marque (affixe) finale régulière de pluriel -en/-in, en ajoutant une syllabe au nom, déplace l’accent d’un cran vers la fin du mot : sing. : ′ argaz (homme) plur. : ir′ gazen (hommes) [...] Dans les items verbaux simples (sans affixes satellites : pronoms personnels régimes ou particules de mouvement) soumis à analyse, l’accent est toujours sur la dernière syllabe : [...] yek′rez = il a labouré… [...] Pour le groupe verbal, sous réserve de vérifications complémentaires, on peut do…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kabyle is not in the catalog. Of the six title-hits, three are Tashlhiyt/Tamazight theses (Jebbour 1996, Iazzi 1991, Moktadir 1989: other variety, not located, priority none), Boukous 1990 'Syllabification…' is unlocated and Boukous 1990 'Pharyngalisation…' (read, Cairn via the Internet Archive) is Tashlhiyt emphasis spreading with no accent content. The one relevant item, Chaker 1995 'Éléments de prosodie kabyle' (Peeters, 97-116), was read in its original 1991 journal form (Études et Documents Berbères 8: 5-25, full text on Cairn, downloaded from an Internet Archive copy; saved with; It is the best first-hand statement: instrumental pilot showing a pitch (F0) accent, non-distinctive, penultimate in nouns and final/last-full-vowel in verb groups, no intrinsic word accent, 'accent quasi fixe'. Also downloaded and read: the Encyclopédie berbère 'Accent' entry (Vycichl & Chaker 1984, OpenEdition open access) summarizing Willms's older noun-initial intensity-accent account with caution; Applegate 1966 (archive.org) teaching equal force on all full-vowel syllables; Gaoua 2023 JASA abstract (initial-syllable intensity/vowel-quality prominence, F0 not a correlate; full paper not found, medium priority); Mettouchi et al. 2007 (HAL) silent on word stress.

[...] L'immense majorité des nominaux (isolés) sont des paroxytons : l'accent porte très régulièrement sur l'avant-dernière syllabe. [...] Dans les items verbaux simples (sans affixes satellites : pronoms personnels régimes ou particules de mouvement) soumis à analyse, l'accent est toujours sur la dernière syllabe [...] le groupe nominal porte régulièrement son accent (principal) sur l'avant-dernière syllabe ; le groupe verbal, sur la dernière voyelle pleine (/a, i, u/), à défaut sur la dernière syllabe du noyau verbal
new_statements.translation: Kabyle has a word accent of a melodic nature. [...] The vast majority of (isolated) nominals are paroxytones: the accent falls very regularly on the penultimate syllable. [...] In the simple verbal items (without satellite affixes: object pronouns or directional particles) submitted to analysis, the accent is always on the last syllable [...] the nominal group regularly bears its (main) accent on the penultimate syllable; the verbal group, on the last full vowel (/a, i, u/), failing that on the last syllable of the verbal nucleus
new_statements.citation: Chaker, Salem (1991). Éléments de prosodie berbère. Quelques données exploratoires. Études et Documents Berbères 8: 5-25. DOI 10.3917/edb.008.0005
new_statements.locator: Section A 'L'accent kabyle', I 'La nature physique de l'accent' (Cairn §15), II 'La position de l'accent': 'Le Nom' (§21-25), 'Le Verbe' (§27-30), summary (§37); also conclusion §91-92. Printed pages within 5-25 (approx. pp. 7-11); exact page not recoverable from the Cairn HTML (paragraph numbers are Cairn's)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Internet Archive copy of the free Cairn full text of Chaker 1991, EDB 8: 5-25). All four fragments of the stitched quote are there verbatim at the stated Cairn paragraphs: §15 "Le kabyle possède un accent de mot de nature mélodique. C'est, pratiquement dans tous les cas (72 sur 77, soit ± 93,5 %), la fréquence fondamentale (F°) qui est le facteur discriminant"; §21 "L'immense majorité des nominaux (isolés) sont des paroxytons : l'accent porte très régulièrement sur l'avant-dernière syllabe" with 'argaz / ir'gazen; §27 "Dans les items verbaux simples (sans affixes satellites : pronoms personnels régimes ou particules de mouvement) soumis à analyse, l'accent est toujours sur la derniè…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-class-conditioned position, realised by pitch (F0), non-contrastive (culminative only): nouns (with their gender/number/state and possessive/deictic affixes) are accented on the penultimate syllable of the whole accent unit (ˈargaz 'man' / irˈgazen 'men'; arˈgaz-is, argaˈz-agi); verbs are accented on the final syllable of the verbal nucleus (yekˈrez), or, when clitics with a full vowel /a i u/ are attached, on the last full vowel of the verb group (kerzen-ˈasen-ten, yefka-ˈyasen). Chaker classes Kabyle as a 'langue à accent quasi fixe' (Garde). If a single position must be chosen for the catalog, the noun rule (penult) is the dominant one (50/56 nouns); the verb rule is final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not established instrumentally ('les données de l'analyse instrumentale ne permettent pas pour l'instant d'établir l'existence de l'accent secondaire qu'évoque A. Willms'); Chaker thinks an 'écho de l'accent' probably exists in complex verb groups with several full-vowel affixes, e.g. yefka-ˈyasen-ˌtn-id.
new_statements.exceptions: 6 of 56 nouns (trisyllabic) were accented on the first syllable, contrary to the rule (Chaker suspects experimental artefacts); plural suffix -en/-in shifts the accent one syllable rightward; full-vowel clitics attract the verbal accent; in enumerative/coordinated sequences the verb accent is attracted to the first syllable of the second verb and nouns are accented on the final; thematised nouns shift the accent to the final syllable. Earlier claim (Willms 1961/1965, reported second-hand): intensity accent on the initial a-/ta- syllable of nouns — explicitly revised by Chaker.
new_statements.domain_note: Accent unit is the noun phrase or verb phrase (nucleus + clitic 'satellites'); data are 77 isolated words/groups read in citation form. Chaker's own conclusion (§91) hedges: 'Il semble qu'il n'y ait pas en kabyle « d'accent de mot intrinsèque », mais simplement un accent de mot en phrase' — the isolated-word accent may just be declarative-sentence intonation. Gaoua 2023 (abstract) reports intensity/duration prominence on initial or penultimate syllables and no F0 correlate, so the description remains contested.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kabyle in general (Chaker's own Grande Kabylie material; no sub-dialect named in the passages read). Chaker 2004 notes the melodic accent is probably specific to Kabyle among Berber varieties. Glottolog language-level kaby1243; the Willms claims reported second-hand also concern Kabyle. Basset & Picard 1948 (list of works to obtain) describes the Irjen variety.

new_statements.quote: Le kabyle possède un accent de mot de nature mélodique. [§15] … L'immense majorité des nominaux (isolés) sont des paroxytons : l'accent porte très régulièrement sur l'avant-dernière syllabe. [§21] … le groupe nominal porte régulièrement son accent (principal) sur l'avant-dernière syllabe ; le groupe verbal, sur la dernière voyelle pleine (/a, i, u/), à défaut sur la dernière syllabe du noyau verbal [§38] … Il semble qu'il n'y ait pas en kabyle « d'accent de mot intrinsèque », mais simplement un accent de mot en phrase. [§91]
new_statements.translation: Kabyle has a word accent of melodic (pitch) nature. … The vast majority of (isolated) nominals are paroxytones: the accent falls very regularly on the penultimate syllable. … the noun group regularly carries its (main) accent on the penultimate syllable; the verb group, on the last full vowel (/a, i, u/), otherwise on the last syllable of the verbal core … It seems that Kabyle has no 'intrinsic word accent', but simply a word accent in the phrase.
new_statements.citation: Chaker, Salem (1991). Éléments de prosodie berbère. Quelques données exploratoires. Études et Documents Berbères 8: 5-25 (DOI 10.3917/edb.008.0005); reprinted as 'Éléments de prosodie kabyle' in Chaker (1995), Linguistique berbère. Études de syntaxe et de diachronie, Peeters, 97-116
new_statements.locator: §15, §21, §38, §91 (Cairn paragraph numbering of the 1991 article; = Chaker 1995: 97-116)
new_statements.reading: Kabyle has no lexical/contrastive stress. Prominence is an F0 peak whose position is fixed by word class within the phrase: penultimate syllable of the noun group (shifting right when suffixes add syllables: ′argaz > ir′gazen, ar′gaz-is), final syllable / last full vowel of the verb group including clitics (ker′zen-ten, kerzen-′asen). Chaker labels it 'accent quasi fixe', culminative and syntactically demarcative, and concludes it is really the declarative-intonation peak rather than a word-level accent. This is the only instrumental, first-hand statement found; it explicitly overturns the older Willms/Basset description (weak intensity accent, noun-initial a-/ta- syllable) repeated in the Encyclopédie berbère 'Accent' entry (1984). Gaoua's 2023 abstract (6 speakers) reports initial-syllable intensity/vowel-quality prominence with no F0 correlate, so the acoustic picture is unsettled; for coding purposes Kabyle looks like 'no fixed lexical stress; phrase-level, category-dependent pitch prominence (noun penult / verb final)'.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: The first problem in reading the transcriptions arises from the position of stress or accent. In those words that are written without hyphens, it is necessary to find one of the three vowel letters a, i, u. Each one of these that occurs in a word without hyphens is pronounced with equal force: axam, Amirik:4ni. [...] When a word is written without vowels, it is necessary to note the syllabic divisions (Supplement I) and to pronounce each syllable with equal force: lmlk [...] If the word contains only one written vowel and several consonants, [...] the syllable containing the written vowel receives the greatest force: ism = i sam. [...] It is important, therefore, to note the positions of hyphens in words, mark the parts indicated by the hyphens, and supply equal stress for each of these parts
new_statements.citation: Applegate, Joseph R. (1966). Spoken Kabyle: a basic course. Washington DC: US Office of Education. 443 pp.
new_statements.locator: Unit I, Notes, §III 'Phonology', pp. 9-10 of the pre-publication draft (archive.org leaves 10-11; printed page = leaf - 1, checked against '- 134 -' on leaf 135); sentence-level remark Unit VII p. 134 (leaf 135)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File lines 578-643 (Unit I, 'III Phonology'). Every clause of the quotation is present verbatim; the only differences are scanned noise ('Amirik:4ni' for amirik:ani, 'lmlk = Y1mi1%k'). Locator verified against 444 leaves): leaf 10 (0-based, archive.org numbering) begins 'III Phonology: In addition to the general pronunciation exercises in Supplement I' and ends 'unless there is a third vowel in the word:'; leaf 11 begins 'axam = a xam lamirik: = la mi rik:' and carries 'receives the greatest force: ism = i sam' and 'supply equal stress for each of these parts'; leaf 135 ends with the printed page marker '134' and carries 'Notice that there is also a change in stress and intonation patterns'…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's existing_statements insofar as both deny a lexical/contrastive word stress (Chaker 1991: 'pas d'accent de mot intrinsèque'; Applegate: all full-vowel syllables 'equal force'). It is silent on Chaker's regular melodic peak (noun-group penult / verb-group final) and on Gaoua's initial-syllable intensity prominence; being an intensity-based learner's instruction with no instrumental data, it neither confirms nor refutes the F0 pattern, but its 'equal force' wording sits closer to 'no word-level prominence' than to any fixed position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A pedagogical reading rule, not an analysis: Kabyle words have no single stressed syllable. Every syllable containing a full vowel (a, i, u) is pronounced with equal force; in words written without full vowels (schwa-only, e.g. lmlk) every syllable gets equal force; when a word has only one full vowel, that syllable gets the greatest force; each hyphen-separated part of a word (stem + affix/clitic) is given equal stress. Separately (p. 134), fronting a constituent for emphasis brings 'a change in stress and intonation patterns' — a sentence-level, not word-level, effect. ('Amirik:4ni' is the scanned of amirik:ani.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the instruction to give 'equal stress' to every hyphen-marked part of a word implies no primary/secondary distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the case of a word with a single full vowel among several consonants, where that vowel's syllable 'receives the greatest force' (ism = i sam). No dialect exceptions; the course says only that it concerns 'the dialects of Kabyle with which we are concerned' (p. ~52), with dialogue material set in Tizi Ouzou (Greater Kabylia).
new_statements.identity_note: Applegate's course is a US Office of Education audiolingual text (ERIC ED 034 198) in a phonemic transcription; it refers only to 'the dialects of Kabyle with which we are concerned' and its dialogues place the speakers in Tizi Ouzou (Greater Kabylia). Chaker's instrumental data (per the on-disk 1995 reprint, p. 115) come from one Greater Kabylia speaker. Boukous 1990 (unopened) is tagged by Glottolog for Tarifit, Tachelhit and Kabyle via an autotranslated EBALL code; his own phonological work is Tashlhiyt-based.

readall_conflicts: Applegate 1966 (equal force on every full-vowel syllable, i.e. no word-level stress position) is compatible with Chaker 1991/1995's conclusion that Kabyle has no intrinsic word accent, but it says nothing about Chaker's category-dependent F0 peak (noun-group penult, verb-group final), and it sits awkwardly with Gaoua's 2023 abstract (initial-syllable intensity/vowel-quality prominence, no F0 correlate) and with the older Willms/Basset noun-initial weak intensity accent repeated in Vycichl & Chaker 1984: Applegate's instruction denies any intensity difference at all. Boukous 1990 could not be opened; his 2009 book (not a listed work) gives a non-contrastive final-syllable tonic accent for 'amazighe' from his own Tashlhiyt intuition, which is not a Kabyle statement and would contradict Chaker's noun-penult peak if applied to Kabyle.

Position is category-dependent and quasi-fixed: nouns penultimate (50/56 = 89.3%; shifts rightward with suffixes: ′argaz / ir′gazen, ar′gaz-is / arga′z-agi), verbs final, or on the last full vowel /a,i,u/ of the verb+clitic group (ker′zen-ten, kerzen-′asen). No secondary accent found. Accent is culminative/demarcative, never distinctive (§8: 'L'accent n'a pas de fonction distinctive fondamentale en berbère'). Concl…

sources.quote: §3 Dans la phrase berbère toutes les syllabes ne sont pas prononcées avec la même intensité, mais ce fait n'implique nullement l'existence d'un accent d'intensité à valeur phonologique. […] §13 Pour les deux dialectes Willms pose un accent d'intensité, sans modification mélodique ou de durée notable et distingue entre un accent principal et un accent secondaire. Sur les mots isolés, la position varie selon la classe grammaticale (verbe ~ nom). Pour les noms, l'accent porterait sur la syllabe initiale dite d'« article » ('a-/'ta-), ce qui paraît être une généralisation à accepter avec prudence.
sources.note: Pan-Berber survey; Vycichl: no phonological pitch accent in Berber, most authors do not mark stress, A. Basset sceptical. Chaker's note on Kabyle reports Willms 1961/1965 second-hand: intensity accent, main + secondary, position varies by word class, nouns accented on the initial 'article' syllable a-/ta- ('généralisation à accepter avec prudence'), enclitics attract the accent.

sources.citation: Gaoua, Dehbia (2023). The status of lexical stress in understudied Kabyle Tamazight-Berber: Acoustic evidence from Kabyle dominant speakers. JASA 153(3 Suppl.): A297 (ASA meeting paper; any associated Boston University dissertation)
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher (DOI); library e-access not checked
sources.quote: Results from a closely controlled acoustic production study of 6 male Kabyle-native speakers, showed some evidence of lexical prominence in root words, which was manifested by intensity, duration (for vowel /æ/), and vowel quality […]. Louder, and higher and more peripheral vowels were observed in initial syllables while longer vowels (/æ/) were found in penultimate syllables. Surprisingly, based on the present data we did not see strong evidence of F0 being a meaningful correlate
sources.note: Most recent controlled acoustic study (6 speakers); its abstract contradicts Chaker on the cue (intensity/duration, not F0) and reports initial vs penultimate prominence; the full paper/dissertation could supersede the 1991 rule.
